content: Between 2014 and June 2015 in Kenya, wheelchair-related training was associated with improved performance in activities of daily living (ADLs). In the Philippines, from February to May 2015, wheelchair training was linked to a higher likelihood of serious falls compared to no falls, but it did not show a significant association with non-serious falls versus no falls. Participants who underwent wheelchair training reported enjoying the experience and expressed willingness to recommend it to others. In Croatia, adult members of the Croatian Paraplegic and Tetraplegic Alliance participated in wheelchair education and skills training, which included wheelchair adjustment, positioning, transfers, and driving. Most participants expressed high satisfaction with the training, and no significant differences were observed between groups trained by medical versus non-medical personnel. In Ireland, a study involving two children with cerebral palsy used computer-generated virtual functional driving tasks (e.g., forward movement, left and right turns, and collision avoidance). Both participants retained the wheelchair driving skills they acquired during the virtual training. In the UK, six novice adult powered wheelchair users with neurological conditions (e.g., traumatic brain injury, brainstem hemorrhage, cerebrovascular accident, and TB meningitis) participated in virtual reality-based training. The training focused on maneuverability and route-finding tasks. The results suggested that virtual environments could be a useful tool for assessing and training novice powered wheelchair users. In the USA, three young children with multiple severe impairments underwent individualized power mobility training using a custom-designed attendant control unit. The training, conducted weekly for 12 weeks, demonstrated improved power mobility performance and participation in daily activities. In Canada, four adults with right cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs) participated in verbal mediation training, which involved saying tasks aloud during wheelchair drills. The training improved their ability to perform wheelchair tasks safely and independently, with fewer errors. In Australia, four children with physical disabilities participated in the Smart Wheelchair Mobility Training Program (SWMTP). The program, based on motor learning theory, improved their driving skills and had a positive impact on their psychosocial outcomes. In the UK and Australia, three children using powered wheelchairs participated in training with smart wheelchairs equipped with sensors. The training enhanced their mobility and allowed for the development of effective training schemes for children with severe and complex disabilities. In the USA, an adult with ataxia underwent 10 sessions of powered wheelchair training in varied environments. The training improved their wheelchair function, and the improvements were sustained after one year. In the UK, an elderly left hemiplegic patient participated in wheelchair transfer training broken into eight steps with verbal mediation. The training improved their task performance and demonstrated the potential of verbal mediation as an adjunct to standard physiotherapy for stroke patients with neglect. In the USA, an 11-month-old infant with cerebral palsy underwent open exploration and prompted mobility training using toys, verbal prompts, and hand-over-hand assistance. The training improved the infant’s mobility success over 14 consecutive weekday sessions. In the USA, an adult with right hemisphere damage and severe cognitive impairment participated in a systematic written transfer program with verbal mediation. The training improved their ability to learn wheelchair transfers. In Canada, 11 older adult manual wheelchair users participated in the peer-led Wheelchair Self-Efficacy Enhanced for Use (WheelSeeU) program. The program consisted of 90-minute peer-led sessions tailored to participants’ goals. The training significantly improved wheelchair skills performance. In Ireland, a study on children with cerebral palsy learning to drive a wheelchair using virtual training showed that computer-generated tasks could improve driving abilities. Retention rates of acquired skills were 58% and 93% for the two participants. In the UK, a study on novice adult powered wheelchair users using virtual environments for training found variable results across measures such as task completion time, distance traveled, and number of collisions. The findings suggested that virtual environments could be a valuable tool for training. In the USA, three children with multiple severe impairments underwent power mobility training. The training had variable effects on their daily activity scores, with one participant showing slight improvement. In Canada, a peer-led manual wheelchair training program significantly improved wheelchair skills performance in adult manual wheelchair users. However, a separate program focusing on wheelchair maintenance skills did not significantly improve mobility outcomes. In the UK, a study on adults with spinal cord injuries found that active rehabilitation with wheelchair skills training significantly improved wheelchair skills. In the USA, a systematic and written transfer program with verbal mediation improved the ability of a patient with severe cognitive impairment to learn wheelchair transfers. In Canada, a study on older adults using manual wheelchairs found that peer-led training programs significantly improved wheelchair skills and self-efficacy.
